content:
If I had to pick an Apple tech moment that epitomises the "Sense and Sensibility" paradox, yesterday's iPhone launch event is it.

Having watched the iPhone Duo portion of yesterday's keynote this morning, I had to wipe drool off my desk, but for me, the real star of the show was the iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max, all thanks to its new photography features…

Variable aperture – with caveats

Given the supply chain required to bring a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it's no surprise this feature was widely leaked ahead of the announcement. The only thing that wasn't entirely clear was whether the feature would appear on both Pro models, or whether it would be exclusive to the Pro Max; the good news is it's the former.

Apple has also confirmed that, although the iPhone will adjust the aperture automatically in some situations, we also have full manual control. As I said before, we may need to temper our expectations about the practical differences this feature will bring.

However, I also speculated that Apple may have improved Portrait Mode on this latest model by essentially combining a wider aperture with computational photography to produce better results than hardware alone could achieve. This remains to be verified, but based on some of the sample images they showed, I have reason to believe I might be right.

I'll try the feature out, and of course I'll share the results.

Low-light photo and video

The maximum aperture has also improved by close to a stop, going from f/1.78 on the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48. While this may not make a huge difference to depth of field itself, it should be a fairly valuable boost for shooting in low-light environments, including night scenes.

Manual shutter speed control

In addition to manual aperture control, we can also choose the shutter speed for both stills and video.

For stills, this means being able to shoot long exposures. The promo video showed how this can be used to create motion blur effects. We don't yet know how long the maximum exposure can be, or whether combining the smallest aperture with computational tricks can achieve a 30-second exposure – the kind of exposure time typically used to render running water into silky smooth effects. The same technique can also be used to make passers-by "disappear" from the frame.

With a traditional camera, this effect would require a neutral density filter (ND filter) to cut the light, but third-party iPhone apps already exist that can composite a series of photos to create a similar image. I personally use an app called Spectre for this all the time.

As for video, manual shutter speed control allows me to apply the 180-degree rule. When shooting at 24 frames per second, we need to set the shutter speed to 1/48 second to achieve the most natural-looking motion blur. This functionality has been available in third-party pro photography apps like Blackmagic Cam for a while, but it's great to now see the same capability in Apple's own app.

White balance control

Another feature that used to be exclusive to third-party apps is white balance control, which has now also made its way into the official app.

For stills photography, this lets us adjust colour temperature to our own taste, but it's most important for video. Automatic white balance means the colour temperature – the entire feel of the image – will drift throughout a clip, creating a very noticeable amateur look. Being able to lock white balance for an entire clip is a major improvement.

Cinematic mode for all video

Cinematic mode is essentially the video equivalent of Portrait mode, allowing us to apply a shallow depth of field effect. Until now, we've had to choose between standard video and Cinematic mode video – although the latter actually still outputs a flat file. The iPhone 18 Pro lets you decide after the fact whether to apply the Cinematic mode effect to standard video.

Additionally, we can now shoot Cinematic mode video at up to 60 frames per second, meaning it can be used for slow motion.

Intelligent focus mode for video

Current iPhones already let you set the focus to track a specific person in the frame, and the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a more advanced version.

Specifically, it appears to use AI to recognise specific individuals, maintaining a stable lock on them even when other people pass between the camera and the subject. Furthermore, even if the subject leaves the frame and re-enters, it can reacquire the lock on them.

Histogram

This feature had been reported before yesterday's keynote, so I'll briefly recap what was said previously.

Battery life

Shooting video is extremely power-hungry, so any improvement in this area is welcome. We don't yet know the specific figures for video, but given that the Pro Max's maximum usage time has increased from 39 hours to 45 hours, we can expect roughly 15% longer shooting times compared to last year's model.

Apple-certified images

Finally, if you need to prove the authenticity of a photograph, there is a way to do so. This is clearly a professional tool, primarily relevant to photojournalists, law enforcement and similar roles.

Summary

Of course, some people's eyes will only be on the iPhone Duo, and that's completely understandable. But if the iPhone is an important part of your camera kit, it's the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max that are the real winners.
